processing: Unoxidised green tea: as with gunpowder tea generally, the leaf is heated to stop oxidation, then rolled into small tight pellets and dried.
harvest_season: No single prized picking is recorded for this style; Sri Lanka's tea districts crop through much of the year, and sellers rarely state a season.
appearance_liquor: Clear yellow with a light green cast, typical of rolled green teas.
appearance_wet: The pellets open into mid-green leaf, usually in pieces and less whole than a fine Chinese pellet tea.
taste_profile: Milder than Chinese gunpowder, with more body than its pale colour suggests and a light oaky note that vendors often mention.

brewing.notes: Normally brewed Western-style. As with other pellet greens, give the leaf room to open and keep the water off the boil to hold back bitterness.

vintage_note: Sold as an undated everyday loose tea, usually under a shop or blend name such as Royal Ceylon Gunpowder, rarely with a harvest date. As with other green teas it is best drunk fresh, within about a year, so a shop with quick turnover matters more than the label.
description:
Ceylon Gunpowder is the Chinese pellet style made on Sri Lankan leaf. Sri Lanka is a black tea country, and its green tea is a small sideline, so this is something of a curiosity rather than a tradition.

The shape comes from rolling the leaf tightly after it has been heated to stop oxidation. Rolling protects the leaf a little in storage and makes it pack small. It says nothing about quality, since pellets are made at every grade.

Sellers consistently describe it as much gentler than Chinese gunpowder, which tends to be smokier and sharper. Expect a fairly full green cup with a woody edge. Water that is too hot brings out bitterness, as it does with most pellet greens, so let the kettle cool first.

Most of what is sold comes through Western tea shops under the Royal Ceylon Gunpowder name, often credited to Dimbula. Few sellers name an estate, so origin claims are hard to check. If you want to know exactly what you are drinking, an estate-named Sri Lankan green is the better buy.
history:
Little is documented about this style in particular. Sri Lankan green tea is itself recent: one Sri Lankan account dates the first export of Ceylon green tea to 1982 and says most of it is now made from Assam stock, mainly in Uva.

The Idulgashinna estate in Uva is described by a retailer as the first in the country to produce green tea, though whether it makes this pellet style is not recorded. Who first rolled gunpowder on the island, and when, remains unknown.
